title: DHS proposes $103,265 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions under new rule
text:
DHS proposes $103,265 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions under new rule
S. M. Holmes
The Trump administration has proposed a permanent rule that would require employers to pay a $103,265 fee for each H-1B cap-subject petition they file to hire highly skilled foreign workers in specialty occupations, according to an Aug. 26 announcement. The proposed rule was published in the Federal Register by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship Immigration Services. Businesses, institutions, and other interested parties have until 11:59 p.m. on Sep. 24 to submit comments on the proposal.
The proposed fee is separate from a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas ordered by President Donald Trump last year, which is currently stayed during a federal court challenge involving 20 states including New Jersey. A federal court in Massachusetts ruled that the earlier fee was illegal, and it is not being enforced while the federal government appeals.
According to the notice in the Federal Register, "Now the Trump administration is using a different mechanism – a proposed regulatory change rather than a presidential proclamation – to establish a 'dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the law immigration system.'"
The new proposed fee does not apply to petitions that are not subject to the agency’s annual cap, such as those filed by U.S. higher education institutions and nonprofit hospitals affiliated with universities and research institutions. The burden of this proposal would fall most heavily on “cap-subject” private employers relying on the annual H-1B lottery process—particularly small businesses and startups for whom $103,265 represents significant resources.
Cap-subject refers to an H-1B petition counting against an annual numerical limit: generally 85,000 are available each fiscal year (65,000 regular plus 20,000 for individuals with advanced degrees). Demand typically exceeds these numbers so affected employers must go through registration and selection processes known as the H-1B lottery; if selected under this proposal they would be required to pay this new fee when filing their petition. The rule does not specify whether fees will be refunded if petitions are denied due to failure meeting requirements.
The New Jersey Business and Industry Association serves as one of New Jersey's largest employer associations representing private-sector employers across various sectors; it facilitates partnerships among businesses, government entities, and academic institutions while providing advocacy services and cost-saving benefits, according to its official website.
